schemas.name: 1RM Calculator
schemas.description: Estimate your one rep max with six formulas, compare their results, and view training percentages. See a worked example and understand strength-reference limits.

acceptedAnswer.text: A one-repetition maximum is the heaviest load you can lift once with the defined technique for an exercise. This calculator estimates it from a completed set. An estimated value is a planning reference and does not confirm that you can safely lift that load today.

There is no universal error margin for every person, exercise and repetition count. Technique, fatigue, effort and muscular endurance can affect an estimate. Record the conditions of the set and follow the trend consistently. Avoid treating an estimated maximum as a load you must attempt.

No formula is guaranteed to be most accurate for every lifter and exercise. This calculator displays six estimates and uses their arithmetic average for its headline. The average does not guarantee reduced bias. Inspect the spread and use the same method when comparing sessions.

Strength standards compare a load with a reference category, often relative to bodyweight and grouped by exercise and sex. They answer a different question from estimating a maximum. The categories provide context, but they cannot determine your personal training readiness, technique quality or recovery needs.

mainEntity.name: How should I use the training percentage table?

acceptedAnswer.text: The table multiplies the estimated maximum by preset percentages. Those loads are starting references rather than guaranteed repetition targets or a complete program. Select working weights according to your plan, technique and current capacity. If the estimate changes, review the underlying set before changing every training load.
